A Private Prosecution

By: Eugene Botha | Delivery

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
You have the right to prosecute a criminal if the state refuses to do so.

Summary:
Private prosecutions are very rare, but if the State refuse to prosecute, a private individual can apply for a licences to launch a private prosecution. This past week a man has been found guilty of murdering his girlfriend nine years ago, after her family succeeded in getting him convicted in a private prosecution.

Further information:
Private prosecutions are very rare, but if the State refuse to prosecute, a private individual can apply for a licences to launch a private prosecution. This past week a man has been found guilty of murdering his girlfriend nine years ago, after her family succeeded in getting him convicted in a private prosecution.


In 2005 Rochelle Naidoo was found dead in her flat with a gunshot wound. Her boyfriend Faizel Hendricks, who was the only other person present there that night, was a suspect.


At the time, Hendricks was arrested and charged with Naidoo’s murder, but he pleaded not guilty and the case was later withdrawn by the director of public prosecutions because the evidence was not strong enough to secure a conviction.


A judicial inquest followed in 2008 when it was suggested Naidoo could have committed suicide, but the inquest determined that the cause of death was not clear.


Her parents were adamant that their daughter had not taken her own life.


It was Hendricks’s case that he had been in Naidoo’s flat when he saw her grab his unlicensed .38 Special Revolver, put the gun in her mouth and pulled the trigger.


They had apparently been seen arguing earlier.


Following the inquest, the Asmalls launched the private prosecution.


Private prosecutions refer to criminal cases initiated by individuals or an organisation and happens after the director of public prosecutions issues a certificate for the individual or the organisation to privately prosecute.


Naidoo’s parents would have had to pay a substantial amount of money - according to legal experts - for the private prosecution to proceed.


They paid a deposit to secure the use of the court and the equipment, instructed Durban senior counsel Gideon Scheltema to prosecute the case, and sought the opinion of Durban ballistics expert Jacobus Steyl and forensic expert Reggie Perumal to prove that something sinister happened to their daughter.


According to Steyl’s evidence, before Naidoo was shot, Hendricks assaulted her by using blunt force to her mouth.


Hendricks chose not to testify in court, although he had testified at the inquest in 2008.
After 9 long years, he was finally found guilty beyond a reasonable doubt on in the Malmesbury Regional Court on Wednesday 19 June 2015, and must return to court on 30 September for sentencing.

Press Release:


Private Prosecution
It’s a highly unusual, expensive and time-consuming process. But, for ordinary people frustrated with the State withdrawing its case against an accused or simply failing to prosecute, the option of running a private prosecution is another means to secure a conviction. Carte Blanche meets a tenacious family that chose this legal route, to see their daughter’s killer recently convicted and sentenced to 15 years in jail – 11 years after her death.


Script:


Sara:
We’ve got closure now. She’s at rest now. And justice was done.
V/O:
Sara Asmall of Pietermaritzburg is referring to her daughter Rochelle, who was cruelly murdered. Sara and husband Yunus brought the murderer to justice themselves. But it took them 11 long years and they had to use an extraordinary legal process: a private prosecution.
Christo:
A private prosecution is a prosecution similar to a criminal prosecution, driven by a private person under certain conditions, under the Criminal Procedures Act.
V/O:
Christo van Schalkwyk an advocate based in Pietermaritzburg, has followed this unusual legal process carefully.

In two thousand and five when twenty five year old Rochelle ran a family store in Cape Town. She and her parents were very close.
Yunus:
Easy-going. She’s just one of those people that you can enjoy yourself with and be happy with.
Sara:
A first-born is always special and she was... she brought so much fun to the family and everybody can remember Rochelle by her smile.
V/O:
Rochelle was living with her boyfriend Faizel Hendricks in her apartment in Cape Town.
Sara:
I never liked him from the first day I saw him. I said Rochelle, he is not for you. But you know, when they fall in love you can’t stop them, you can’t choose their partners for them.
V/O:
Then, on the twenty eighth of June two thousand and five, Yunus and Sara’s lives changed forever.
Yunus:
We were watching TV in the TV lounge and the phone rang and I took the call and it was Faizel’s brother and he tells me there has been an accident. So I said: “I she injured?” He said “No, she is dead”.
Derek link:
This was the news that every parent dreads. Their daughter Rochelle was found in her Cape Town apartment with a gun lying next to her body.
V/O:
Rochelle had died of a single gunshot. Faizel told the police that she had committed suicide by putting this gun into her mouth and pulling the trigger. The Asmalls refused to accept this explanation and were suspicious.
Yunus:
It was not her nature or demeanour to do a thing like that because a week after that she was actually due to come home and I spoke to her the day before she got murdered and she just told me she’s excited about coming home.
V/O:
The police initiated a suicide investigation. Three weeks later, with little progress being made, the distraught family brought in two private forensic experts: Pathologist Dr Reggie Perumal and ballistics and blood spatter expert Cobus Steyl.

This is the empty flat as they found it. Here Cobus found evidence that the police had overlooked.
Cobus:
On the wall adjacent to a door leading to the room were a pattern of blood. 32 drops of blood impact spatter.
V/O:
The yellow circle indicates where Rochelle was found. On the wall and floor next to the dustbin Cobus found the blood spatter.
Cobus:
I painstakingly worked through them and worked out what the angles were, that means where they originated from to determine a conversion point. Once I determined that I realised there is a problem.
V/O:
Cobus concluded that the blood spatter was as a result of blunt force trauma, not the gunshot. He says the spatter occurred when Rochelle was hit twice in the face while sitting down on this kitchen chair -- away from where she was shot. Reggie agreed.
Reggie:
The gunshot wound was at the back of the mouth but she had injuries outside of the gunshot wound. She had lacerations around the mouth, on the lips. These injuries are not related to the discharge of the firearm.
V/O:
Rochelle also had a wound to her left hand.
Reggie:
That is clearly a defence wound.
V/O:
Her jaw was also fractured. The police surmised that it was caused by the discharge of the gun in her mouth. Cobus disagreed. He filmed these tests with the murder weapon and they revealed that the recoil does not have nearly enough force to have broken Rochelle’s jaw. The damage was caused by blows to her face.
Reggie:
We couldn’t wish these things away. They are there. So having factored all of those things, it did not point to suicide.
V/O:
It pointed to murder. Then Cobus found further evidence the police had missed – there was a CCTV camera and footage of the parking lot. It revealed that the night before the murder Rochelle did not go to her apartment.
Derek:
She slept the night in the car?
Yunus:
She slept the night in the car. He was in the flat and she was in the car. She had come from work and she was terrified to go inside. That’s what it seemed.
V/O:
The next day she leaves for work… returns in the afternoon. She finds Faizel on his way out… she runs after him… they both return and go into the flat. Her face has no injuries to her face.
Cobus:
And from then on we know that it is most probably the time during that period from six o’clock to eight o’clock that the incident occurred.
V/O:
The evidence pointed to an altercation where Faizel first assaulted and then killed Rochelle. In 2008 an inquest was held.
Derek:
So you thought Faizel would be charged and go to court.
Yunus:
Yes, I did.
Derek:
But the Magistrate found that the evidence was inconclusive and referred it back to the NPA and the police.
Yunus:
Yes, and that is where it ended.
DEREK LINK:
Despite the evidence the NPA declined to prosecute Faizel. We asked the NPA in the Western Cape why they did not proceed. In a written statement they replied: “In light of the magistrate’s findings and after carefully evaluating the evidence contained in the docket and the inquest proceedings, the Director of Public Prosecutions… was of the opinion that there remained no reasonable prospect of a successful prosecution.”
V/O:
The Asmalls disagreed. They felt the evidence was overwhelming. And so, in an extraordinary move, they decided to institute a private prosecution and prosecute Faizel themselves.
Yunus:
And we as a family decided that we’ll go that way because we certainly believed that she wouldn’t do anything like that to herself.
Derek:
Christo, how does one institute a private prosecution?
Christo:
First you get a certificate nolle prosequi from the DPP, obviously in the area where the offence was committed. He has to decline to prosecute in the normal course. Second, once you have that, you have the door key, you provide security. Security that you would prosecute and security for possible costs of the accused. Then you are set. And then your prosecution starts as if it is a normal prosecution.
LINK
The only difference was that the Asmalls’ advocate acted as prosecutor, while the NPA monitored the proceedings throughout. Organizing everything took time and court proceedings eventually commenced in 2010, 5 years after the murder.
V/O:
But the wheels of justice turned very slowly. The trial dragged on for many years.
Sara:
It has taken a strain for the eleven years, I mean you must imagine time and again the same thing over and over, but I sat through it, and prayed there as I sat.
Derek:
And you’ve got all the delays and all the postponements?
Sara:
And the worst thing is to sit in court and see his face all the time, you know. For eleven years I watched him there.
V/O:
Christo is not surprised that the trial took so long.
Christo:
Unfortunately it’s not all that rare. Criminal matters themselves, unless it is a systematic delay are prone to systemic delays. Non-availability of personnel, witnesses, all sort of difficulties, and sometimes there is no power in court.
V/O:
In court the very same forensic evidence that was presented at the inquest was again put forward. However, this time round the outcome was very different. In July twenty fourteen Faizel Hendricks was found guilty of murder. But the case was not over. He was yet to be sentenced. Until then Faizel was still a free man.
DEREK LINK:
After the guilty verdict the NPA wanted to intervene and take over the case. However, the Asmalls requested the NPA not to intervene and asked that they be allowed to finalize the proceedings through to the sentencing.
V/O:
The NPA agreed. But it took another two years before Magistrate Michelle Adams could rule.
Derek Link:
And then it was Friday the 13th of May this year. The day of sentencing.
Derek question:
The sentence of 15 years?
Sara:
I’m happy with that sentence and he was put immediately into prison which was good.
Derek link:
With this legal history was made in South Africa. It was the first time a private prosecution for murder succeeded in our courts. The process cost the Asmalls a small fortune but they might get some of it back.
Christo:
The Criminal Procedure Act says that if you’re successful, the court may order the accused, now the convicted accused, to pay some of your costs. A second proviso would be the court may also under certain circumstances order the State to pay some of your costs.
V/O:
But this is not important to Yunus and Sara. What they did, they did to honour their first-born.
Sara:
After 11 years of going through all this trials and tribulations I’ve closed the book now. Eventually, finally closed the book. And she is in peace. She is resting in peace. Finally.

Her parents were adamant that their daughter had not taken her own life. It was Hendricks’s case that he had been in Naidoo’s flat when he saw her grab his unlicensed .38 Special Revolver, put the gun in her mouth and pulled the trigger. They had apparently been seen arguing earlier. Following the inquest, the Asmalls launched the private prosecution. Private prosecutions refer to criminal cases initiated by individuals or an organisation and happens after the director of public prosecutions issues a certificate for the individual or the organisation to privately prosecute. Naidoo’s parents would have had to pay a substantial amount of money - according to legal experts - for the private prosecution to proceed. They paid a deposit to secure the use of the court and the equipment, instructed Durban senior counsel Gideon Scheltema to prosecute the case, and sought the opinion of Durban ballistics expert Jacobus Steyl and forensic expert Reggie Perumal to prove that something sinister happened to their daughter. According to Steyl’s evidence, before Naidoo was shot, Hendricks assaulted her by using blunt force to her mouth. Hendricks chose not to testify in court, although he had testified at the inquest in 2008. After 9 long years, he was finally found guilty beyond a reasonable doubt on in the Malmesbury Regional Court on Wednesday 19 June 2015, and must return to court on 30 September for sentencing.
